        <span class="ir-badge"><i class="fas fa-skull-crossbones"></i> Incident Response</span>
        <h1>Ransomware Response Playbook 2026</h1>
        <p style="color: var(--text-muted); font-size: 1.1rem;">Complete incident response guide for ransomware
            attacks: containment, negotiation decisions, recovery, and hardening</p>
        <div style="margin-top: 1rem; color: var(--text-muted);">
            <span><i class="fas fa-book-open"></i> 25 min read</span> <span style="margin: 0 0.5rem;">|</span>
            <span><i class="fas fa-crosshairs"></i> Intermediate</span> <span style="margin: 0 0.5rem;">|</span>
            <span><i class="far fa-calendar-alt"></i> January 2026</span>
        </div>
    </div>

    <img src="/images/guides/ransomware-response-playbook.png" alt="Ransomware Response Playbook"
        class="featured-image"
        style="width: 100%; max-width: 100%; height: auto; border-radius: 12px; margin: 2rem 0; box-shadow: 0 10px 40px rgba(255, 61, 61, 0.2); border: 1px solid var(--border);" loading="lazy">

    <div class="warning-box">
        <strong><i class="fas fa-exclamation-triangle"></i> Time is Critical:</strong> The first 60 minutes after
        ransomware detection determine your recovery success. Have this playbook ready BEFORE an incident occurs.
        Print it, distribute it, and practice it.
    </div>

    <!-- Table of Contents -->
    <div class="toc">
        <h3><i class="fas fa-list-ul"></i> Table of Contents</h3>

            <li><a href="#hardening">8. Post-Incident Hardening</a></li>
        </ul>
    </div>

    <h2 id="understanding">1. Understanding Modern Ransomware</h2>

    <p>Modern ransomware is not simple malware. Today's attacks are sophisticated, multi-stage operations run by
        organized criminal enterprises with help desks, negotiators, and affiliate programs.</p>

    <h3>The Evolution of Ransomware</h3>

    <table>
        <thead>
            <tr>
                <th>Era</th>
                <th>Characteristics</th>
                <th>Example</th>
            </tr>
        </thead>
        <tbody>
            <tr>
                <td><strong>2013-2016</strong></td>
                <td>Spray-and-pray, low ransoms</td>
                <td>CryptoLocker</td>
            </tr>
            <tr>
                <td><strong>2017-2019</strong></td>
                <td>Targeted attacks, higher ransoms</td>
                <td>WannaCry, NotPetya</td>
            </tr>
            <tr>
                <td><strong>2020-2022</strong></td>
                <td>Double extortion (encrypt + leak)</td>
                <td>Maze, REvil</td>
            </tr>
            <tr>
                <td><strong>2023-2024</strong></td>
                <td>Triple extortion (+ DDoS/customer targeting)</td>
                <td>LockBit, BlackCat</td>
            </tr>
            <tr>
                <td><strong>2025-2026</strong></td>
                <td>RaaS maturity, AI-assisted attacks</td>
                <td>RansomHub, Akira</td>
            </tr>
        </tbody>
    </table>

    <h3>Common Attack Vectors in 2026</h3>

    <table>
        <thead>
            <tr>
                <th>Vector</th>
                <th>Percentage</th>
                <th>Prevention</th>
            </tr>
        </thead>
        <tbody>
            <tr>
                <td><strong>Phishing/Social Engineering</strong></td>
                <td class="severity-critical">36%</td>
                <td>Security awareness, email filtering</td>
            </tr>
            <tr>
                <td><strong>Exploited Vulnerabilities</strong></td>
                <td class="severity-high">29%</td>
                <td>Patch management, vuln scanning</td>
            </tr>
            <tr>
                <td><strong>Stolen Credentials</strong></td>
                <td class="severity-high">24%</td>
                <td>MFA, credential monitoring</td>
            </tr>
            <tr>
                <td><strong>RDP/VPN Compromise</strong></td>
                <td class="severity-medium">8%</td>
                <td>ZTNA, MFA, monitoring</td>
            </tr>
            <tr>
                <td><strong>Supply Chain</strong></td>
                <td class="severity-medium">3%</td>
                <td>Vendor assessment, SBOM</td>
            </tr>
        </tbody>
    </table>

    <div class="info-box">
        <strong><i class="fas fa-lightbulb"></i> Think of it like this:</strong> Modern ransomware groups operate
        like legitimate businesses. They have customer service, payment portals, and even satisfaction guarantees.
        This professionalization makes them more dangerous and more predictable.
    </div>

    <h2 id="detection">2. Detection and Initial Response</h2>

    <h3>Signs of Active Ransomware</h3>

    <ul>
        <li><i class="fas fa-exclamation-triangle" style="color: var(--accent-red);"></i> <strong>Ransom notes
                appearing</strong> on desktops or in folders</li>
        <li><i class="fas fa-exclamation-triangle" style="color: var(--accent-red);"></i> <strong>File extensions
                changing</strong> to .encrypted, .locked, .crypted, etc.</li>
        <li><i class="fas fa-exclamation-triangle" style="color: var(--accent-orange);"></i> <strong>Unusual
                CPU/disk activity</strong> during off-hours</li>
        <li><i class="fas fa-exclamation-triangle" style="color: var(--accent-orange);"></i> <strong>Security tools
                disabled</strong> or alerting on tampering</li>
        <li><i class="fas fa-exclamation-triangle" style="color: var(--accent-orange);"></i> <strong>Network
                connections</strong> to unusual IPs/domains</li>
        <li><i class="fas fa-exclamation-triangle" style="color: var(--accent-purple);"></i> <strong>Shadow copies
                deleted</strong> (vssadmin commands)</li>
    </ul>

    <h3>First 15 Minutes Checklist</h3>

    <div class="checklist">
        <ul>
            <li>Confirm it is ransomware (not a drill, not a prank)</li>
            <li>DO NOT shut down affected systems (preserve memory evidence)</li>
            <li>Disconnect affected systems from network (pull cables, disable WiFi)</li>
            <li>Take photos of ransom notes and any visible IOCs</li>
            <li>Activate incident response team</li>
            <li>Start incident documentation log</li>
            <li>Notify CISO/IT leadership</li>
            <li>Secure backup systems (take offline if not already)</li>
        </ul>
    </div>

    <div class="warning-box">
        <strong><i class="fas fa-exclamation-triangle"></i> Critical Warning:</strong> DO NOT attempt to decrypt
        files yourself, run anti-malware scans, or engage with attackers without proper preparation. Each of these
        actions can destroy evidence or worsen your position.
    </div>

    <h2 id="containment">3. Containment Phase</h2>

    <p>The goal of containment is to stop the bleeding without destroying evidence.</p>

    <h3>Network Containment Actions</h3>

    <div class="phase-box containment">
        <h4><i class="fas fa-network-wired"></i> Immediate Network Actions</h4>
        <ol>
            <li><strong>Isolate affected VLANs</strong> - Block lateral movement at the switch level</li>
            <li><strong>Disable compromised accounts</strong> - Reset passwords for affected users</li>
            <li><strong>Block C2 domains/IPs</strong> - Update firewall rules immediately</li>
            <li><strong>Disconnect WAN links</strong> if multiple sites affected</li>
            <li><strong>Preserve DNS logs</strong> - Critical for identifying scope</li>
        </ol>
    </div>

    <h3>Endpoint Containment</h3>

    <pre><code># Windows - Isolate endpoint while preserving evidence

Option 1: Block all network except management

netsh advfirewall set allprofiles firewallpolicy blockinbound,blockoutbound

Option 2: Use EDR to quarantine

CrowdStrike: Contain host from console

Defender: Isolate device from portal

Collect volatile evidence FIRST

winpmem.exe memory.raw # Memory dump wmic process list full > processes.txt netstat -ano > connections.txt

    <h3>What NOT to Do During Containment</h3>

    <table>
        <thead>
            <tr>
                <th>Avoid This</th>
                <th>Why It Is Dangerous</th>
            </tr>
        </thead>
        <tbody>
            <tr>
                <td>Shutting down systems</td>
                <td>Destroys memory evidence, may trigger deadman switches</td>
            </tr>
            <tr>
                <td>Running AV scans immediately</td>
                <td>May delete ransomware before analysis, alter timestamps</td>
            </tr>
            <tr>
                <td>Restoring from backups immediately</td>
                <td>May restore infected files, wastes time if scope unknown</td>
            </tr>
            <tr>
                <td>Contacting attackers without preparation</td>
                <td>Shows desperation, weakens negotiation position</td>
            </tr>
        </tbody>
    </table>

    <h2 id="assessment">4. Impact Assessment</h2>

    <p>Before deciding on recovery strategy, you must understand the full scope of the attack.</p>

    <h3>Scope Assessment Checklist</h3>

    <table>
        <thead>
            <tr>
                <th>Question</th>
                <th>How to Determine</th>
                <th>Impact on Response</th>
            </tr>
        </thead>
        <tbody>
            <tr>
                <td>How many systems affected?</td>
                <td>EDR console, manual survey</td>
                <td>Scale of recovery effort</td>
            </tr>
            <tr>
                <td>What data was encrypted?</td>
                <td>File server scans, share analysis</td>
                <td>Business criticality</td>
            </tr>
            <tr>
                <td>Was data exfiltrated?</td>
                <td>Firewall logs, DLP alerts</td>
                <td>Double extortion risk</td>
            </tr>
            <tr>
                <td>How long were they inside?</td>
                <td>SIEM analysis, forensics</td>
                <td>Backup viability</td>
            </tr>
            <tr>
                <td>Are backups clean?</td>
                <td>Isolated backup testing</td>
                <td>Recovery feasibility</td>
            </tr>
            <tr>
                <td>What ransomware variant?</td>
                <td>Ransom note, file extension</td>
                <td>Decryptor availability</td>
            </tr>
        </tbody>
    </table>

    <h3>Identify the Ransomware</h3>

    <p>Knowing the variant helps determine:</p>
    <ul>
        <li>Whether free decryptors exist (check NoMoreRansom.org)</li>
        <li>The group's reputation for providing working decryptors</li>
        <li>Typical ransom amounts and negotiation patterns</li>
        <li>Known TTPs to help identify scope</li>
    </ul>

    <div class="success-box">
        <strong><i class="fas fa-check-circle"></i> Resource:</strong> ID Ransomware
        (id-ransomware.malwarehunterteam.com) can identify the variant from a ransom note or encrypted file sample.
    </div>

    <h2 id="decision">5. The Ransom Decision Framework</h2>

    <p>The question everyone dreads: should you pay? There is no universal answer, but this framework helps
        structure the decision.</p>

    <div class="warning-box">
        <strong><i class="fas fa-exclamation-triangle"></i> Legal Notice:</strong> Paying ransoms to sanctioned
        entities is illegal (OFAC). Always involve legal counsel and check the group against sanctions lists before
        any payment consideration.
    </div>

    <h3>Factors Against Paying</h3>

    <table>
        <thead>
            <tr>
                <th>Factor</th>
                <th>Consideration</th>
            </tr>
        </thead>
        <tbody>
            <tr>
                <td><i class="fas fa-times-circle" style="color: var(--accent-red);"></i> Viable backups exist</td>
                <td>Recovery without payment is possible</td>
            </tr>
            <tr>
                <td><i class="fas fa-times-circle" style="color: var(--accent-red);"></i> Decryptor available</td>
                <td>NoMoreRansom.org has free tool</td>
            </tr>
            <tr>
                <td><i class="fas fa-times-circle" style="color: var(--accent-red);"></i> Group unreliable</td>
                <td>Known for not providing keys</td>
            </tr>
            <tr>
                <td><i class="fas fa-times-circle" style="color: var(--accent-red);"></i> Sanctions risk</td>
                <td>Group on OFAC list</td>
            </tr>
            <tr>
                <td><i class="fas fa-times-circle" style="color: var(--accent-red);"></i> Insurance prohibits</td>
                <td>Policy does not cover ransom</td>
            </tr>
        </tbody>
    </table>

    <h3>Factors That May Support Paying</h3>

    <table>
        <thead>
            <tr>
                <th>Factor</th>
                <th>Consideration</th>
            </tr>
        </thead>
        <tbody>
            <tr>
                <td><i class="fas fa-exclamation-triangle" style="color: var(--accent-orange);"></i> Life-safety
                    data</td>
                <td>Healthcare, infrastructure critical data</td>
            </tr>
            <tr>
                <td><i class="fas fa-exclamation-triangle" style="color: var(--accent-orange);"></i> No viable
                    backups</td>
                <td>Rebuild would be catastrophic</td>
            </tr>
            <tr>
                <td><i class="fas fa-exclamation-triangle" style="color: var(--accent-orange);"></i> Business
                    continuity threat</td>
                <td>Company survival at stake</td>
            </tr>
            <tr>
                <td><i class="fas fa-exclamation-triangle" style="color: var(--accent-orange);"></i> Data exposure
                    risk</td>
                <td>Sensitive data will be leaked</td>
            </tr>
        </tbody>
    </table>

    <h3>If You Decide to Negotiate</h3>

    <ol>
        <li><strong>Engage professional negotiators</strong> - Many cyber insurance policies include this</li>
        <li><strong>Buy time</strong> - Claim complexity, ask for extensions</li>
        <li><strong>Verify capability</strong> - Request proof of decryption for small file</li>
        <li><strong>Negotiate price</strong> - Initial demands are often negotiable by 50-70%</li>
        <li><strong>Use cryptocurrency safely</strong> - Work with reputable exchange</li>
        <li><strong>Get everything in writing</strong> - Screen captures of all communications</li>
    </ol>

    <h2 id="recovery">6. Recovery and Restoration</h2>

    <h3>Recovery Priority Framework</h3>

    <div class="phase-box recovery">
        <h4><i class="fas fa-layer-group"></i> Tier 1 - Critical (0-4 hours)</h4>
        <ul>
            <li>Domain Controllers</li>
            <li>DNS/DHCP servers</li>
            <li>Authentication systems</li>
            <li>Core network infrastructure</li>
        </ul>
    </div>

    <div class="phase-box eradication">
        <h4><i class="fas fa-layer-group"></i> Tier 2 - Essential (4-24 hours)</h4>
        <ul>
            <li>Email systems</li>
            <li>Primary business applications</li>
            <li>Customer-facing systems</li>
            <li>Database servers</li>
        </ul>
    </div>

    <div class="phase-box lessons">
        <h4><i class="fas fa-layer-group"></i> Tier 3 - Important (24-72 hours)</h4>
        <ul>
            <li>File servers</li>
            <li>Development environments</li>
            <li>Secondary applications</li>
            <li>User workstations</li>
        </ul>
    </div>

    <h3>Clean Rebuild vs. Restore</h3>

    <table>
        <thead>
            <tr>
                <th>Approach</th>
                <th>When to Use</th>
                <th>Pros/Cons</th>
            </tr>
        </thead>
        <tbody>
            <tr>
                <td><strong>Clean Rebuild</strong></td>
                <td>Widespread infection, backdoors suspected</td>
                <td><i class="fas fa-check-circle" style="color: var(--accent-green);"></i> Eliminates
                    persistence<br><i class="fas fa-times-circle" style="color: var(--accent-red);"></i>
                    Time-consuming</td>
            </tr>
            <tr>
                <td><strong>Restore from Backup</strong></td>
                <td>Clean backup verified, limited scope</td>
                <td><i class="fas fa-check-circle" style="color: var(--accent-green);"></i> Faster recovery<br><i
                        class="fas fa-times-circle" style="color: var(--accent-red);"></i> May restore malware</td>
            </tr>
            <tr>
                <td><strong>Hybrid Approach</strong></td>
                <td>Most common - rebuild OS, restore data</td>
                <td><i class="fas fa-check-circle" style="color: var(--accent-green);"></i> Balance of
                    speed/security</td>
            </tr>
        </tbody>
    </table>

    <h3>Validation Before Reconnection</h3>

    <p>Before bringing systems back online:</p>

    <div class="checklist">
        <ul>
            <li>All indicators of compromise (IOCs) scanned and cleared</li>
            <li>All credentials reset (especially service accounts)</li>
            <li>Security patches applied to rebuilt systems</li>
            <li>EDR/AV fully operational and updated</li>
            <li>MFA enabled on all accounts</li>
            <li>Monitoring/alerting configured</li>
        </ul>
    </div>

    <h2 id="communication">7. Communication and Notification</h2>

    <h3>Internal Communication Timeline</h3>

    <table>
        <thead>
            <tr>
                <th>When</th>
                <th>Audience</th>
                <th>Message</th>
            </tr>
        </thead>
        <tbody>
            <tr>
                <td>Immediately</td>
                <td>IR Team, CISO</td>
                <td>Incident declared, containment underway</td>
            </tr>
            <tr>
                <td>Within 1 hour</td>
                <td>Executive team, Legal</td>
                <td>Situation brief, business impact</td>
            </tr>
            <tr>
                <td>Within 4 hours</td>
                <td>All employees</td>
                <td>What is happening, what to do/not do</td>
            </tr>
            <tr>
                <td>Ongoing</td>
                <td>Board (if significant)</td>
                <td>Status updates per governance requirements</td>
            </tr>
        </tbody>
    </table>

    <h3>External Notification Requirements</h3>

    <table>
        <thead>
            <tr>
                <th>Regulation</th>
                <th>Deadline</th>
                <th>Trigger</th>
            </tr>
        </thead>
        <tbody>
            <tr>
                <td>GDPR (EU)</td>
                <td class="severity-critical">72 hours</td>
                <td>Personal data breach</td>
            </tr>
            <tr>
                <td>SEC (US Public Co.)</td>
                <td class="severity-critical">4 business days</td>
                <td>Material cybersecurity incident</td>
            </tr>
            <tr>
                <td>HIPAA (Healthcare)</td>
                <td class="severity-high">60 days</td>
                <td>PHI breach affecting 500+</td>
            </tr>
            <tr>
                <td>State Laws (varies)</td>
                <td class="severity-high">24-72 hours</td>
                <td>Resident data exposed</td>
            </tr>
            <tr>
                <td>CIRCIA (Critical Infra)</td>
                <td class="severity-critical">72 hours</td>
                <td>Significant cyber incident</td>
            </tr>
        </tbody>
    </table>

    <div class="info-box">
        <strong><i class="fas fa-lightbulb"></i> Tip:</strong> Pre-draft notification templates as part of your IR
        planning. Under pressure, you will not write well. Legal should review these templates annually.
    </div>

    <h2 id="hardening">8. Post-Incident Hardening</h2>

    <p>After recovery, do not just return to normal. Use this crisis to drive security improvements the organization
        might otherwise resist.</p>

    <h3>Immediate Hardening (Week 1-2)</h3>

    <div class="checklist">
        <ul>
            <li>Reset ALL passwords organization-wide (including service accounts)</li>
            <li>Enable MFA on all accounts (no exceptions)</li>
            <li>Review and restrict administrative privileges</li>
            <li>Implement application whitelisting on critical servers</li>
            <li>Update and test backup procedures</li>
            <li>Deploy enhanced endpoint protection</li>
        </ul>
    </div>

    <h3>Medium-Term Improvements (Month 1-3)</h3>

    <ul>
        <li><strong>Network segmentation</strong> - Limit lateral movement capability</li>
        <li><strong>Zero Trust implementation</strong> - Verify before trusting any connection</li>
        <li><strong>Enhanced email security</strong> - Advanced phishing protection</li>
        <li><strong>Privileged Access Management</strong> - Vault and rotate sensitive credentials</li>
        <li><strong>24/7 Security Operations</strong> - MDR or internal SOC coverage</li>
    </ul>

    <h3>Lessons Learned Process</h3>

    <p>Within 2 weeks of recovery, conduct a formal post-incident review:</p>

    <table>
        <thead>
            <tr>
                <th>Question</th>
                <th>Purpose</th>
            </tr>
        </thead>
        <tbody>
            <tr>
                <td>How did attackers get in?</td>
                <td>Fix the initial access vector</td>
            </tr>
            <tr>
                <td>Why was it not detected earlier?</td>
                <td>Improve detection capabilities</td>
            </tr>
            <tr>
                <td>What slowed our response?</td>
                <td>Improve response processes</td>
            </tr>
            <tr>
                <td>What worked well?</td>
                <td>Reinforce successful practices</td>
            </tr>
            <tr>
                <td>What do we need that we did not have?</td>
                <td>Budget justification</td>
            </tr>
        </tbody>
    </table>

    <div class="success-box">
        <strong><i class="fas fa-check-circle"></i> Key Takeaway:</strong> A ransomware incident is traumatic, but
        organizations that treat it as a learning opportunity emerge stronger. Use the crisis to drive the security
        investments that were previously too expensive.
    </div>
